CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
52-year-old male who presented to his primary care provider on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. He denies any trouble with headaches in the past. Headaches are located behind the eyes and described as a dull nagging ache. Onset was gradual, beginning approximately three months ago. Initial severity was 3/10, which has progressively worsened to 6/10. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning and last a few hours at a time. Patient reports nothing makes them better or worse. Pain does not radiate. Recently patient has noticed bumping into door frames. Tried Tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did not work, so he stopped. Workup for worsening headaches with brain MRI and serology incidentally revealed a pituitary lesion. Patient is now referred by Dr. Henry Howard for possible surgical intervention.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies feeling sick, fever, rashes, or neck stiffness. Denies numbness, tingling, or syncope. Denies change in vision (eyes were checked in the fall). Denies balance issues. Reports recently bumping into door frames.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Patient reports no medical problems. Past clinical history is unremarkable.

MEDICATIONS
No current medications. Tried Tylenol a few times for headaches but discontinued.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient was adopted and has no knowledge of family history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a small house. Denies alcohol use, smoking, and recreational drug use, stating he has never done any of these.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal, motor, or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity is normal. Eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Labs dated 3/3/21 including CBC, CMP, coagulation studies, and CRP are all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH with all other results normal. MRI brain with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals a well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Pituitary adenoma, appearing benign but diagnosis to be confirmed with pathology of removed adenoma. Patient is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression. Surgical intervention indicated. Plan for transsphenoidal approach, which is minimally invasive and goes through the sphenoid sinus. Risks of anesthesia discussed including heart attack, stroke, and death. Risks of surgery discussed including infection, need for further surgery, wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection which may require prolonged hospitalization or additional procedures, seizure, stroke, permanent numbness, weakness, difficulty speaking, or death. Referral to ophthalmology for visual field test prior to surgery to map peripheral vision. Will obtain pre-operative visual field test for comparison after surgery to monitor for vision improvement. Patient will be scheduled fairly quickly. Surgery scheduler Deborah will coordinate surgical scheduling and visual field testing on way out. Patient instructed to call with any questions.
